fields.definition: The practice of recording a part twice (double-tracking) and keeping both takes panned to the center of the stereo image, so the two performances reinforce one another to thicken and strengthen a central element such as a lead vocal or main line.
fields.plain_english: It means playing or singing the same part twice and putting both takes in the middle. The two copies stack up to make that part sound fuller and stronger.
fields.purpose_function: It thickens and reinforces a central part without spreading it wide, so a lead vocal or main line sits solid in the middle of the mix.
fields.practical_application: To beef up a lead vocal, an engineer records a second identical take and keeps both centered so the vocal sounds fuller.
common_mistakes: Thinking a copy-and-paste of one take gives the same thickening as a real second performance
Spreading the two takes wide when the goal is a solid center
Doubling a part that is already busy, which muddies the middle of the mix
scenario_contexts: Double-tracking a lead vocal and keeping both takes centered for a fuller sound
Stacking two center guitar takes to strengthen a main riff
Reinforcing a synth bass line by centering a doubled take

fields.definition: A guitar part placed in the center of the stereo image—often a rhythm or lead layer—that anchors the arrangement while other guitars are panned left and right for width.
fields.plain_english: It is a guitar part set in the middle of the mix, not to the left or right. It gives the song a solid guitar center while other guitars sit out to the sides.
fields.purpose_function: It anchors the guitar arrangement in the middle so the song has a strong central foundation, leaving the sides open for panned parts.
fields.practical_application: When layering guitars, an engineer keeps the main rhythm part centered and pans the doubles left and right to build width around it.
common_mistakes: Centering several loud guitars at once, which crowds the middle with the vocal and bass
Forgetting to pan the supporting guitars, so the whole guitar section stacks in the center
Confusing a single centered layer with a fully mono guitar mix
scenario_contexts: Keeping a main rhythm guitar centered while panning its doubles wide
Placing a lead guitar in the center to sit with the vocal
Anchoring an acoustic layer in the middle of a dense rock mix

fields.definition: Harmony vocal or instrumental parts placed in the center of the stereo image rather than panned to the sides, keeping the supporting harmony aligned directly with the lead.
fields.plain_english: It means putting harmony parts in the middle of the mix instead of out to the sides. The harmony then lines up right behind the lead voice.
fields.purpose_function: It keeps harmony parts tight against the lead so they support it directly, useful when a solid central blend matters more than stereo width.
fields.practical_application: For a close vocal blend, an engineer keeps the harmony stacks centered under the lead rather than spreading them left and right.
common_mistakes: Piling many centered harmonies onto the lead, which clutters the middle
Assuming centered harmony always sounds better than panned harmony
Letting a centered harmony fight the lead for the same space
scenario_contexts: Keeping a two-part harmony centered under a lead vocal for a tight blend
Centering a background vocal to thicken the lead without adding width
Placing a harmony line in the middle so it stays glued to the melody

fields.definition: The sense of room and space captured or added around a recorded choir—from natural room reflections and reverberation picked up by distant or ambient microphones, or from added reverb—that conveys the acoustic environment the ensemble sings in.
fields.plain_english: It is the roomy, echoing sound around a choir. It comes from the real space the choir sings in, or from added reverb, and it makes the singing feel like a live hall.
fields.purpose_function: It places the choir in a believable space and adds a sense of size and blend, so the voices sound like a unified group in a room rather than dry and close.
fields.practical_application: To capture choir ambience, an engineer sets a pair of room mics back from the group, or adds hall reverb to the close mics in the mix.
common_mistakes: Placing ambient mics too far back, so the choir sounds distant and washed out
Adding heavy reverb to tracks that are already ambient, which smears the words
Ignoring the room's own sound and expecting reverb plug-ins to fix a dead space
scenario_contexts: Setting room mics in a church to capture the natural ambience of a choir
Adding hall reverb to close-miked choir tracks to restore a sense of space
Balancing close and ambient choir mics for the right amount of room sound

sources: DPA Microphones technical documentation (choir and ensemble miking)

fields.definition: The use of mix automation—recorded moves of level, mute, panning, or plug-in settings over time—applied to choir tracks so their balance and processing follow the changing dynamics of an arrangement.
fields.plain_english: It means setting the mixer to change the choir's volume and settings on its own as the song plays. The moves are saved once and then repeat exactly every time.
fields.purpose_function: It lets an engineer ride the choir's level and effects through a song—up in the choruses, down under a solo—without redoing fader moves by hand on every pass.
fields.practical_application: An engineer draws fader automation so the choir swells in the final chorus and drops back during the verses.
common_mistakes: Writing jumpy automation moves that cause audible level steps
Automating each choir channel when one subgroup fader would do the job
Forgetting that a later manual fader move can overwrite the written automation
scenario_contexts: Automating a choir swell into the last chorus of a song
Pulling the choir down automatically under a lead vocal line
Muting the choir bus automatically in sections where it does not sing

fields.definition: The degree to which individual voices in a choir merge into a single, unified sound rather than standing out separately, shaped by the singers' balance and tuning and by recording choices such as microphone type and distance.
fields.plain_english: It is how well the singers' voices melt together into one smooth sound. Good blend means you hear a single choir, not a bunch of separate voices.
fields.purpose_function: It creates the impression of one cohesive ensemble, so the choir reads as a unified section instead of a set of competing soloists.
fields.practical_application: To improve blend, an engineer backs the mics off a little and lets the singers balance themselves in the room before capturing them.
common_mistakes: Close-miking individual singers, which breaks up the natural blend
Expecting the mix to fix a blend the choir never achieved in the room
Boosting one section so hard that it pulls out of the ensemble
scenario_contexts: Using a distant stereo pair so a choir blends into one sound
Arranging singers by section to improve blend before recording
Balancing the choir sections so no single part sticks out

sources: DPA Microphones technical documentation (choir and ensemble miking)

fields.definition: The application of dynamic-range compression to a choir recording, reducing the difference between its loudest and softest passages so the ensemble sits at a steadier level in the mix.
fields.plain_english: It means using a compressor to even out how loud a choir gets. It gently turns down the loudest parts so soft and loud passages stay closer in volume.
fields.purpose_function: It controls the wide dynamics of a choir so quiet passages stay audible and loud swells do not jump out, helping the choir sit consistently in a mix.
fields.practical_application: An engineer puts gentle bus compression on the choir subgroup to smooth its dynamics before setting its level in the mix.
common_mistakes: Using a fast, heavy setting that pumps and pulls up room noise between phrases
Squashing the choir so hard it loses its natural swells and expression
Compressing on the channels and again on the bus until the sound is lifeless
scenario_contexts: Applying gentle compression to a choir bus to even out its dynamics
Taming loud choral swells so they do not overpower a lead vocal
Keeping soft choir passages audible in a dense mix

fields.definition: The use of a de-esser—a frequency-selective compressor targeting the sibilant range—to reduce harsh "s," "sh," and "t" sounds on a choir recording, where many voices singing consonants together can build up exaggerated sibilance.
fields.plain_english: It means taming the harsh, hissy "s" sounds in a choir recording. A de-esser turns down just those sharp sounds when many singers hit an "s" at once.
fields.purpose_function: It softens exaggerated sibilance that piles up when a whole choir sings consonants together, keeping the top end smooth without dulling the overall tone.
fields.practical_application: When a choir's "s" sounds turn harsh, an engineer inserts a de-esser tuned to the sibilant range and eases the level of those peaks.
common_mistakes: Setting the de-esser too strong, which gives the choir a lisping, dull sound
Targeting the wrong frequency, so the sibilance is not actually reduced
Cutting all the highs with broad EQ instead of de-essing only the harsh peaks
scenario_contexts: De-essing a close-miked choir where the "s" sounds have piled up
Smoothing harsh consonants on a choir bus in a bright mix
Taming sibilance on layered choir stacks before adding reverb

fields.definition: The sense of front-to-back distance and layering in a recorded choir, created by the placement of singers and microphones and by cues such as level, ambience, and reflection that make some voices seem nearer and others farther away.
fields.plain_english: It is the feeling of near and far in a choir recording, the sense that some voices sit closer and some sit deeper back. It makes the choir sound three-dimensional instead of flat.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a choir a realistic three-dimensional space, so the ensemble sounds layered from front to back rather than pinned to one flat plane.
fields.practical_application: An engineer builds depth by blending close mics with a distant ambient pair, letting reflections and level place the sections at different distances.
common_mistakes: Using only close mics, which flattens the choir with no sense of distance
Adding reverb but no level or ambience cues, so the depth still sounds fake
Placing every section at the same distance, which loses front-to-back layering
scenario_contexts: Blending close and distant mics to give a choir front-to-back depth
Using room reflections to place back rows farther away than the front
Layering ambience so a choir sounds three-dimensional in a mix

sources: DPA Microphones technical documentation (choir and ensemble miking)
